text: Observer is about 1.4 AU from the black hole when Earth is a quarter orbit away from it (scenario geometry: sqrt of 2 AU).
as_written: about one point four times the distance from you to the Sun
source: Scenario geometry (Earth and black hole each 1 AU from the Sun at right angles); AU defined by IAU 2012 Resolution B2

text: Scenario black hole has about ten solar masses, similar to Gaia BH1.
as_written: roughly ten times the mass of the Sun
source: Scenario assumption, chosen near the mass of Gaia BH1 (El-Badry et al. 2023, MNRAS 518, 1057)

text: Scenario speed of the black hole is 30 km/s.
as_written: moving at thirty kilometres every second
source: Scenario assumption

text: A 10 solar mass black hole has an event horizon about 59 km across (Schwarzschild diameter 4GM/c^2).
as_written: only about sixty kilometres across
source: Schwarzschild solution; solar GM from IAU 2015 Resolution B3; speed of light from CODATA

text: At 30 km/s the hole crosses its own ~59 km width in about two seconds.
as_written: every two seconds
source: Arithmetic: 59 km divided by 30 km/s

text: Gaia BH1 is about 1,560 light years away.
as_written: about fifteen hundred and sixty light years away
source: El-Badry et al. 2023, MNRAS 518, 1057, Gaia astrometry

text: Gaia BH1 has a mass of about 9.6 solar masses.
as_written: about nine point six Suns
source: El-Badry et al. 2023, MNRAS 518, 1057

text: Gaia BH3 was announced in 2024.
as_written: announced in 2024
source: Gaia Collaboration 2024, A&A 686, L2

text: Gaia BH3 is about 1,900 light years away.
as_written: about nineteen hundred light years away
source: Gaia Collaboration 2024, A&A 686, L2 (about 590 parsecs)

text: Gaia BH3 has a mass of about 33 solar masses.
as_written: about thirty three Suns
source: Gaia Collaboration 2024, A&A 686, L2 (32.7 solar masses)

text: The Milky Way is estimated to hold on the order of 100 million stellar-remnant black holes, with large uncertainty.
as_written: something like a hundred million black holes
source: Elbert, Bullock & Kaplinghat 2018, MNRAS 473, 1186

text: Scholz's star passed the Sun roughly 70,000 years ago.
as_written: roughly seventy thousand years ago
source: Mamajek et al. 2015, ApJ Letters 800, L17

text: Scholz's star passed at about 0.8 light years (about 52,000 AU).
as_written: about eight tenths of a light year
source: Mamajek et al. 2015, ApJ Letters 800, L17

text: That distance is around 50,000 AU.
as_written: around fifty thousand times the distance from Earth to the Sun
source: Mamajek et al. 2015, ApJ Letters 800, L17 (52,000 AU)

text: Stars in the Sun's neighbourhood move relative to one another at tens of km/s.
as_written: tens of kilometres per second
source: Schonrich, Binney & Dehnen 2010, MNRAS 403, 1829; Gaia Collaboration stellar kinematics

text: Closest approach to the Sun is one astronomical unit.
as_written: one astronomical unit from the Sun
source: Scenario assumption; AU defined by IAU 2012 Resolution B2

text: One AU is about 150 million km.
as_written: a hundred and fifty million kilometres
source: IAU 2012 Resolution B2 (149,597,870,700 m)

text: Schwarzschild radius is about 2.95 km per solar mass.
as_written: about two point nine five kilometres for every solar mass
source: Schwarzschild radius 2GM/c^2 with IAU 2015 Resolution B3 solar GM

text: A ten solar mass hole has a horizon radius of about 30 km.
as_written: about thirty kilometres in radius
source: Schwarzschild radius 2GM/c^2

text: At 1.4 AU a 10 solar mass hole pulls Earth about five times as hard as the Sun does.
as_written: about five times harder than the Sun does
source: Newtonian gravity, mass ratio 10 and distance ratio 1.41 squared, IAU 2015 B3 solar GM

text: Gravity on the space station is about 90 percent of surface gravity.
as_written: about ninety percent
source: NASA, microgravity explainer

text: The tide from the hole at this distance is only somewhat stronger than the Moon's.
as_written: only somewhat stronger than the Moon's
source: Newtonian tidal acceleration 2GMR/r^3 for the hole at 1.4 AU versus the Moon at 384,400 km (NASA Moon Fact Sheet); about 1.6 times

text: Gravitational lensing was first measured at the 1919 solar eclipse.
as_written: solar eclipse of 1919
source: Dyson, Eddington & Davidson 1920, Phil. Trans. R. Soc. A 220, 291

text: The Einstein ring for this lens would be a few arcminutes across, about one seventh of the Moon's roughly 31 arcminute width.
as_written: a few arcminutes across, about a seventh the width of the full Moon
source: Einstein ring formula for a 10 solar mass lens at 1.4 AU; Moon angular size from NASA Moon Fact Sheet

text: Sunlight takes about 8 minutes 20 seconds to reach Earth.
as_written: eight minutes and twenty seconds
source: NASA; 499 seconds light travel time for 1 AU

text: The Sun's radius is about 696,000 km.
as_written: six hundred and ninety six thousand kilometres
source: IAU 2015 Resolution B3 nominal solar radius, 695,700 km

text: One AU is more than 200 solar radii.
as_written: more than two hundred times farther away
source: IAU 2012 B2 and IAU 2015 B3; ratio is about 215

text: At equal distance, a ten solar mass hole pulls the Sun ten times harder than the Sun pulls Earth.
as_written: ten times harder than the Sun pulls Earth
source: Newton's law of gravitation, mass ratio

text: Measured from the Sun, Earth's extra acceleration in this geometry is about eight times the Sun's usual pull.
as_written: about eight times as strong as the Sun's usual pull
source: Vector sum of Newtonian accelerations in the scenario geometry, about 0.047 against 0.0059 metres per second squared; IAU 2015 B3 solar GM

text: Neptune's orbital period is about 165 years.
as_written: one hundred and sixty five years
source: NASA Neptune Fact Sheet (164.8 years)

text: At 30 km/s the hole travels 108,000 km per hour.
as_written: one hundred and eight thousand kilometres every hour
source: Arithmetic: 30 km/s times 3600 s

text: With a constant 0.047 m/s^2 relative push, Earth is displaced about 300 km after one hour.
as_written: about three hundred kilometres off its old path
source: Kinematics, half a t squared, using the Newtonian estimate above

text: After six hours the displacement is about 11,000 km, near Earth's diameter of about 12,700 km.
as_written: roughly eleven thousand kilometres, close to the width of the planet
source: Kinematics using the same estimate; Earth diameter from NASA Earth Fact Sheet

text: In one day the hole moves about 2.6 million km, nearly seven Moon distances.
as_written: about two point six million kilometres, nearly seven times the distance to the Moon
source: Arithmetic: 30 km/s times 86,400 s; Moon mean distance 384,400 km from NASA Moon Fact Sheet

text: The extra push would change Earth's velocity by about 4 km/s in a day.
as_written: about four kilometres per second
source: Newtonian estimate, 0.047 m/s^2 times 86,400 s

text: Earth orbits the Sun at about 30 km/s.
as_written: Earth circles the Sun at about thirty kilometres per second
source: NASA Earth Fact Sheet (29.78 km/s)

text: Solar escape speed at Earth's distance is about 42 km/s.
as_written: is about forty two
source: Square root of two times Earth's orbital speed, NASA Earth Fact Sheet

text: Earth is about 12,700 km wide.
as_written: about twelve thousand seven hundred kilometres wide
source: NASA Earth Fact Sheet (12,742 km)

text: The Moon orbits at about 384,000 km.
as_written: about three hundred and eighty four thousand kilometres out
source: NASA Moon Fact Sheet (384,400 km)

text: The relative path of the Sun and hole bends by about 165 degrees in this encounter.
as_written: about a hundred and sixty five degrees
source: Two-body hyperbolic deflection, eccentricity about 1.009 for periapsis 1 AU, 30 km/s, 11 solar masses; deflection equals 2 arcsin of 1 over e

text: The close approach lasts about two months (1 AU at 30 km/s is about 58 days).
as_written: about two months
source: Arithmetic: 1.496e8 km divided by 30 km/s

text: Mercury's orbital period is about 88 days.
as_written: eighty eight days
source: NASA Mercury Fact Sheet (87.97 days)

text: Jupiter's orbital period is nearly 12 years.
as_written: nearly twelve years
source: NASA Jupiter Fact Sheet (11.86 years)

text: Flyby simulations find that planets well outside the closest approach distance are the most exposed, and that flybys within a few times a planet's orbital distance eject or strongly perturb it.
as_written: a flyby that comes within a few times a planet's orbital distance tends to throw it onto a stretched orbit or out of the system entirely
source: Heggie & Rasio 1996, MNRAS 282, 1064; Spurzem et al. 2009, ApJ 697, 458

text: The Sun orbits the galaxy about once every 230 million years.
as_written: two hundred and thirty million years or so
source: Binney & Tremaine, Galactic Dynamics (2008); literature values range from about 210 to 250 million years

text: The Sun's galactic orbital speed is about 220 km/s.
as_written: about two hundred and twenty kilometres per second
source: Binney & Tremaine, Galactic Dynamics (2008); other measurements give up to about 240 km/s

text: Galactic escape speed at the Sun's position exceeds 500 km/s.
as_written: more than five hundred kilometres per second
source: Piffl et al. 2014, A&A 562, A91 (about 533 km/s)

text: At 30 km/s the hole is about 6 AU away after one year.
as_written: about six astronomical units away
source: Arithmetic: 30 km/s times 3.156e7 s is about 6.3 AU

text: After a decade it is about 63 AU away.
as_written: about sixty three
source: Arithmetic: 6.3 AU per year times 10

text: After about 16 years it is around 100 AU, beyond Neptune at about 30 AU.
as_written: After about sixteen years
source: Arithmetic; Neptune distance from NASA Neptune Fact Sheet

text: An Earth flung out at about 30 km/s is about 7 AU from the Sun after a year, where sunlight is less than one fiftieth as strong.
as_written: less than a fiftieth of what it was
source: Inverse-square law

text: At about 64 AU the Sun would be about 100 times brighter than the full Moon.
as_written: about a hundred times brighter than the full Moon
source: Inverse-square law from the Sun's apparent magnitude of minus 26.74 and the full Moon at about minus 12.7 (NASA fact sheets)

text: At roughly 64 AU after a decade of 30 km/s travel.
as_written: roughly sixty four astronomical units
source: Arithmetic: 1 AU plus 63 AU

text: The average ocean depth is about 3.7 km.
as_written: about three point seven kilometres deep
source: NOAA (mean ocean depth 3,688 m)

text: Earth's internal heat flow is about 47 terawatts.
as_written: about forty seven trillion watts
source: Davies & Davies 2010, Solid Earth 1, 5-24

text: That is under a thousandth of the sunlight Earth intercepts, about 170,000 terawatts.
as_written: less than a thousandth of what sunlight used to deliver
source: Solar constant of about 1361 W per square metre (Kopp & Lean 2011, Geophys. Res. Lett.) times Earth's cross-section

text: Radiating 47 TW from Earth's surface gives an equilibrium temperature near 35 K, about minus 238 Celsius.
as_written: near thirty five kelvin
source: Stefan-Boltzmann law with Davies & Davies 2010 heat flow, emissivity 1

text: 35 K is about minus 238 degrees Celsius.
as_written: about two hundred and thirty eight degrees below zero Celsius
source: Unit conversion

text: Nitrogen freezes at about 63 kelvin.
as_written: about sixty three kelvin
source: NIST Chemistry WebBook (triple point 63.15 K)

text: Frozen atmosphere spread evenly would be roughly ten metres deep.
as_written: roughly ten metres deep
source: Atmospheric mass about 5.15e18 kg (Trenberth & Smith 2005, J. Climate) over Earth's area of about 5.1e14 square metres, at solid-air density near 1000 kg per cubic metre

text: Hydrothermal vent communities were found at the Galapagos Rift in 1977.
source: Corliss et al. 1979, Science 203, 1073

text: Microbes live in coal beds about 2.5 km below the seafloor.
as_written: about two and a half kilometres below the seafloor
source: Inagaki et al. 2015, Science 349, 420 (IODP Expedition 337)

text: The Oort cloud may hold about a trillion icy bodies.
as_written: perhaps a trillion of them
source: NASA Solar System Exploration, Oort Cloud

text: The Oort cloud's outer edge is perhaps 100,000 AU.
as_written: perhaps a hundred thousand astronomical units
source: NASA Solar System Exploration, Oort Cloud

text: At 30 km/s, crossing about 100,000 AU takes roughly 16,000 years.
as_written: about sixteen thousand years
source: Arithmetic: 100,000 AU times 58 days per AU

text: A body falling from 50,000 AU takes about two million years to reach the Sun.
as_written: fifty thousand astronomical units takes about two million years
source: Kepler's third law: half the period of an orbit with semi-major axis 25,000 AU

text: Batygin and Brown proposed Planet Nine in 2016.
source: Batygin & Brown 2016, Astronomical Journal 151, 22

text: Planet Nine was proposed as about ten Earth masses.
as_written: perhaps ten times the mass of Earth
source: Batygin & Brown 2016, Astronomical Journal 151, 22

text: Some analyses argue the clustering of distant objects is an observational bias.
as_written: Some analyses argue the clustering is just a trick of where telescopes have happened to look
source: Napier et al. 2021, Planetary Science Journal 2, 59

text: Scholtz and Unwin proposed the primordial black hole idea in 2019.
as_written: Then in 2019
source: Scholtz & Unwin, arXiv 1909.11090, published in Phys. Rev. Lett. 125, 051103 (2020)

text: The proposed black hole has about five Earth masses.
as_written: about five times the mass of Earth
source: Scholtz & Unwin 2020, Phys. Rev. Lett. 125, 051103

text: A five Earth mass black hole has a Schwarzschild radius of about 4.4 cm.
as_written: about four and a half centimetres
source: Schwarzschild radius 2GM/c^2 with Earth's GM of 3.986e14 m^3/s^2, about 8.87 mm per Earth mass

text: That corresponds to a diameter under ten centimetres.
as_written: under ten centimetres across
source: Same calculation, diameter about 8.9 cm

text: OGLE reported very short microlensing events hinting at Earth-mass objects; their nature is debated.
as_written: a handful of odd, very short microlensing events, seen by a survey called OGLE
source: Mroz et al. 2017, Nature 548, 183; Niikura et al. 2019, Phys. Rev. D 99, 083503

text: Rubin Observatory's Legacy Survey of Space and Time is a ten year survey.
as_written: ten year survey
source: Ivezic et al. 2019, ApJ 873, 111; Vera C. Rubin Observatory

text: At 30 km/s a light year takes roughly ten thousand years to cross.
as_written: roughly ten thousand years
source: Arithmetic: speed of light divided by 30 km/s is about 9,990

text: The first isolated black hole candidate was detected by microlensing in 2022, with differing mass estimates between teams.
as_written: by microlensing in 2022
source: Sahu et al. 2022, ApJ 933, 83; Lam et al. 2022, ApJ Letters 933, L23
